S: Here to talk through the MRI. Hepatology told him it is liver cancer, 5 cm, single, and that a transplant is the treatment they are aiming for. Transplant center intake call done, first visit in February. He is scared but wants to go forward. Belly still full; hepatology bumped nothing. Eating small meals, weight steady since December. Sleep poor, mood "up and down"; no hopelessness, no thoughts of self-harm.

- HCC in Child-Pugh C cirrhosis: transplant evaluation in progress. I will help coordinate records (his cancer history - rectal 2020/21, prostate 2017, skin 2023 - will matter to them; sent our records).

LIVER TRANSPLANT PROGRAM, 02/20/2024
Re: Peter Kimball, 68
Mr. Kimball was seen to begin liver transplant evaluation for hepatocellular carcinoma (single 5.0 cm LI-RADS 5 lesion, AFP 400) in Child-Pugh C cirrhosis from treated hepatitis C and prior alcohol use, abstinent since 2017.
His other cancers (prostate 2017 in remission; rectal adenocarcinoma 2020, resected 2021 without recurrence; cutaneous SCC excised 2023) and his PAD, COPD and asbestosis require full review by our committee. Locoregional bridging treatment is not advised with his liver function.
Next steps: cardiopulmonary testing, oncology input on recurrence risk, social work and nutrition evaluations.
Transplant Hepatology

documents.title: Office Visit

S: For about two months, episodes of upper abdominal pain, dull, coming and going over hours, no clear trigger. Weight still drifting down. About a week and a half ago a vein on the inside of his left forearm became sore and red, like a cord; it is fading on its own. No fever. No black stools, bleeding rare. No new confusion.
O: Vitals as charted. Jaundiced, thin. Abd distended, mild epigastric tenderness, no rebound. L forearm: faint residual redness along a superficial vein, minimal tenderness, no swelling of the arm. Basilar crackles.
A: Episodic abdominal pain and weight loss in a man with HCC and cirrhosis, plus a spontaneous superficial thrombophlebitis without a line or injury. Concerned about a second process (pancreas or GI) rather than the liver alone.
P: CMP/CBC today. Called GI - seen 8/23. Hepatology and transplant copied. Return for spreading redness or arm swelling.

events.reason: Abdominal pain, weight loss, migratory thrombophlebitis

orders.order: MRI abdomen with gadolinium, pancreas protocol

documents.title: Gastroenterology consultation
documents.author: gastroenterology
documents.body:
GASTROENTEROLOGY, 08/23/2024
Mr. Kimball comes back to us, nine months after his hepatology diagnosis of HCC, with intermittent abdominal pain and continued weight loss. Over two weeks his left arm veins were tender and red and then settled on their own; now the same thing has started over the right side of his chest. Background: radiation proctitis (APC 12/2022), Child-Pugh C cirrhosis, HCC under transplant evaluation.
Family history: father died of pancreatic adenocarcinoma at 72; paternal uncle colorectal cancer; brother prostate cancer; mother emphysema.
Social: 40 pack-years, quit 2017; no alcohol since 2017.
Allergies: sulfonamides, iodinated contrast.

Exam: along the superficial veins of the right chest wall, a palpable cord with redness and tenderness. Abdomen soft, not distended, no masses, no enlargement of liver or spleen on my exam.

Labs: Hgb 12.1, WBC 7.8, platelets 305, fasting glucose 156, CA 19-9 120 U/mL, CEA 5.2 ng/mL.

Impression: migratory superficial thrombophlebitis with a raised CA 19-9 and weight loss - concerning for an occult pancreatic malignancy (Trousseau phenomenon), especially with his father's history.
Plan: MRI abdomen with gadolinium (pancreas protocol; no iodinated contrast), then EUS with FNA of any lesion.
Gastroenterology

reports.study: MRI abdomen with and without contrast
reports.text: Pancreas protocol MRI with gadolinium. Pancreatic body: 2.6 cm hypoenhancing mass with upstream pancreatic duct dilatation. Pancreatic head and tail otherwise unremarkable. Known right hepatic lobe mass, 5.0 cm, unchanged in size and enhancement pattern. No new liver lesion. Ascites. No adenopathy.
reports.conclusion: 2.6 cm pancreatic body mass, highly suspicious for adenocarcinoma. Known right lobe HCC unchanged at 5.0 cm.

Pathology (09/20): adenocarcinoma.

documents.title: Oncology consultation - pancreatic cancer
documents.author: oncology
documents.body:
MEDICAL ONCOLOGY, 09/26/2024
Mr. Kimball is known to us from his rectal cancer. EUS-FNA of a 2.6 cm pancreatic body mass shows adenocarcinoma; CA 19-9 120. He also has a 5 cm HCC in Child-Pugh C cirrhosis (bilirubin about 3, albumin under 3, INR 1.5-1.6).
Assessment: pancreatic adenocarcinoma. Resection is not possible with his liver disease, and standard chemotherapy regimens are not safe with Child-Pugh C function and this bilirubin. We talked at length; he understands the treatment options are limited and wants to focus on staying as well as he can.
Plan: supportive care, symptom management, oncology visits every 2-3 months with CA 19-9 and imaging as needed. We will let the transplant program know. Palliative care resources discussed and offered.
Medical Oncology

events.reason: Follow-up after pancreatic cancer diagnosis; advance care planning

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, high MDM

documents.title: Office Visit - advance care planning
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
S: Pancreatic cancer confirmed by EUS last month; oncology says no surgery and no chemo with his liver. He expects the transplant program to close his evaluation. Abdominal pain episodes manageable with his oxycodone, 2-3/day. Chest-wall vein soreness gone. Appetite small.
ACP (30 min, pt alone, by his choice): He understands his illnesses are not curable. What matters: staying at home, staying clear-headed, not being on machines. He would want treatment of things that can be fixed (an infection, a blockage) if he could get back to home afterward. Does not want CPR or a breathing tube if his heart or breathing stops. Completed a health care proxy form today and will tell us who he chose; MOLST discussed and he wants to think more before signing.
PHQ-9 6: sad at times, sleeping poorly, no suicidal thoughts.
O: Vitals as charted. Thin, jaundiced. Abd distended, mild epigastric tenderness. Basilar crackles. No asterixis.
A/P:
- Pancreatic adenocarcinoma, HCC, decompensated cirrhosis: supportive care with oncology/hepatology. Code preferences documented as above.
- Pain: current oxycodone dosing adequate; told him to call if he needs more than 4/day.
- DM2: with less food, watch for lows; glargine stays 24 for now.
- Flu (HD) and updated COVID today.
RTC 2 months.

documents.title: Oncology visit - back pain
documents.author: oncology
documents.body:
MEDICAL ONCOLOGY, 03/05/2025
Thank you for the heads-up about his back. Mr. Kimball, with pancreatic adenocarcinoma, HCC and a history of rectal and prostate cancers, returns with three months of dull low-back pain that is worse at night and does not ease with rest.
Exam: focal tenderness over the T10 spinous process. Mild weakness of both legs. Light-touch sensation reduced below the level of the umbilicus. Rectal tone not tested.
Labs: calcium 11.2 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 140 U/L, PSA 0.2 ng/mL, Hgb 12.5 g/dL.
MRI thoracic spine the same afternoon (no contrast): T10 metastasis with an epidural component contacting the cord, no cord signal change, no fracture.

Impression: metastatic carcinoma to bone at T10 with epidural extension and early neurologic signs; hypercalcemia of malignancy. Most likely pancreatic in origin; PSA remains low, making prostate unlikely. Biopsy would not change treatment and was not pursued.
Plan:
1. Dexamethasone 10 mg IV today, then 4 mg every 6 hours with a taper over four weeks.
2. Urgent radiation oncology: palliative radiation to T10 begins tomorrow, 30 Gy in 10 fractions.
3. Zoledronic acid 3.5 mg IV (dose adjusted for kidney function) tomorrow, then every 12 weeks. Oral hydration.
4. Glucose will rise on steroids - he will use his correction-scale lispro; PCP copied.
5. Return immediately for worse weakness, numbness or incontinence.
Medical Oncology

documents.title: Emergency department record
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT RECORD, 09/02/2025 (received with hospital records)
CC: right upper quadrant pain, fever and vomiting.
HPI: 69-year-old man with pancreatic adenocarcinoma metastatic to bone, HCC and decompensated cirrhosis from hepatitis C. For 24 hours, severe right upper abdominal pain, constant and sharp, going through to the right shoulder, with fever and repeated vomiting.
Allergies: sulfonamides; iodinated contrast (anaphylaxis).
Vitals: T 38.9 C (102 F), HR 110, BP 135/85.
Exam: marked right upper quadrant tenderness with a positive Murphy sign.
Labs: white count elevated with a left shift.
Imaging: ultrasound - gallstones with gas in the gallbladder wall. CT abdomen without contrast - gas in the gallbladder wall and in the pericholecystic area.
Impression: acute emphysematous cholecystitis.
ED course: IV fluids, blood cultures, IV piperacillin-tazobactam, IV analgesia, antiemetic. General surgery and interventional radiology consulted. Admitted to surgery.

documents.title: Discharge summary - cholecystitis
documents.author: general surgery
documents.body:
DISCHARGE SUMMARY
Admitted 09/02/2025, discharged 09/08/2025.
Diagnosis: acute emphysematous cholecystitis with cholelithiasis.
Background: pancreatic adenocarcinoma with bone metastasis, HCC, Child-Pugh C cirrhosis, CKD 3a, insulin-treated diabetes.
Course: Surgery judged him too high risk for cholecystectomy given Child-Pugh C cirrhosis and metastatic cancer, in line with his stated wishes. Interventional radiology placed a percutaneous cholecystostomy tube under ultrasound guidance on 09/03. IV piperacillin-tazobactam continued; fever settled by 09/05 and pain improved. Diet advanced. Lactulose and rifaximin continued; no encephalopathy. Insulin adjusted while eating little, back to home doses at discharge.
Discharge medications: home medications unchanged, plus amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg twice daily to complete 14 days of antibiotics (through 09/16).
Drain: flush daily, record output. IR follow-up in 6 weeks for cholangiogram and possible removal.
Code status: DNR/DNI per patient.
Follow-up: IR, oncology, PCP.

documents.title: Discharge summary - C. difficile colitis with toxic megacolon
documents.author: hospital medicine
documents.body:
DISCHARGE SUMMARY
Admitted 03/06/2026 - discharged 03/20/2026. ICU 03/09 - 03/13.
Principal diagnosis: Clostridioides difficile infection complicated by toxic megacolon.
Presentation: 70-year-old man (pancreatic adenocarcinoma with bone metastasis, HCC, Child-Pugh C cirrhosis, chronic radiation proctitis, emphysematous cholecystitis in September) with five days of watery diarrhea, cramping abdominal pain and low-grade fever, two weeks after completing clindamycin for pneumonia. Admission vitals: T 38.2 C (100.8 F), BP 110/70, HR 102, RR 22. WBC 18.0, Hgb 13.2, platelets 250, creatinine 1.2, BUN 28. Stool C. difficile toxin positive. Oral vancomycin 125 mg four times daily started 03/06.
Hospital course: On the third day of vancomycin his diarrhea stopped, but he became more lethargic, with fever to 39.4 C (102.9 F) and heart rate 120. Abdomen distended and diffusely tender without rebound or guarding; bowel sounds hypoactive. Repeat WBC 25.0. Abdominal radiograph: marked colonic distension without free air. Transferred to the ICU 03/09 with toxic megacolon. Treated as fulminant C. difficile: vancomycin 500 mg four times daily by nasogastric tube, vancomycin retention enemas, IV metronidazole 500 mg every 8 hours, bowel rest, IV fluids. General surgery consulted daily; given his Child-Pugh C cirrhosis, metastatic cancer and stated wishes (DNR/DNI, would accept treatment aimed at returning home), colectomy was not pursued while he improved. Distension resolved on serial films by 03/12; returned to the floor 03/13. Diet resumed; stools formed by discharge. WBC 9.6 on 03/20. No encephalopathy; lactulose held in the ICU and resumed at a lower dose, then back to his home titration.
Discharge medications: home medications unchanged; vancomycin 125 mg by mouth four times daily through 03/31/2026.
Allergies: sulfonamides, iodinated contrast. Add: avoid clindamycin if possible.
Follow-up: PCP and oncology in 1-2 weeks; return for recurrent diarrhea, fever or abdominal swelling.

documents.title: Message from patient
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Last day of the vancomycin is tomorrow. Bowels are ok, 3 a day back on the lactulose. Oncology saw me Friday. I'm worn out and don't feel like another trip right now - is it ok if I skip coming in? I'll call if the diarrhea comes back.

documents.title: Reply
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Thanks for the update, Peter. The PCP has read your hospital records. Finish the vancomycin, and call us the same day if you have watery diarrhea again, fever or a swollen belly - C. diff can come back after treatment. We'll leave a follow-up up to you; just call when you'd like to be seen.

Recovering slowly after the March admission for C. difficile with toxic megacolon; no recurrence of diarrhea since finishing vancomycin. Back pain controlled. Zoledronic acid continues every 12 weeks. Supportive care; next visit in 3 months.
